n: The civil war drags on, but the momentum is clearly with David. This one verse summarizes years of slow change: God’s chosen king rises while Saul’s dynasty fades.

f.g: Waxed = grew, became.

n: The narrator pauses to list David’s sons born in Hebron. Several of them — Amnon, Absalom, Adonijah — will become central, and tragic, figures later in the story.
Absalom’s mother was a princess of Geshur, a small Aramean kingdom northeast of the Sea of Galilee. That royal connection will matter when Absalom later flees there.

f.g: Called Daniel in 1 Chronicles 3:1; he never appears again in the story.

n: Adonijah, the fourth son, will later try to seize the throne before Solomon.
Six sons by six different wives. Multiplying wives was a common royal practice for building alliances, but the law of Moses warned kings against it, and these rival households will bring heartache.

f.w: These were born to David in Hebron

n: Meanwhile, Abner is steadily strengthening his own position inside Saul’s house. He is the real power behind Ish-bosheth’s throne.
Ish-bosheth accuses Abner of sleeping with Saul’s concubine Rizpah. In that culture, taking a former king’s concubine could signal a claim to his throne, so this was a serious charge.

f.g: A secondary wife with lower legal status than a full wife.
A Hebrew idiom for sexual relations.

n: Abner explodes in anger. After all his loyalty to Saul’s family, does Ish-bosheth treat him like a worthless traitor over a woman?

f.g: An insult meaning “Am I a contemptible nobody?” Dogs were scavengers and despised in ancient Israel.
Wroth = very angry.

n: Abner swears a solemn oath that he will help bring about what God had promised David. It reveals that even Saul’s side knew of God’s promise.

f.w: So do God to Abner, and more also
f.g: A standard oath formula: “May God punish me severely if I don’t do this.”

f.w: as the LORD hath sworn to David

n: He vows to transfer the whole kingdom to David, from the far north to the far south.

f.g: Here translate = transfer.
A phrase meaning the entire land of Israel, from its northernmost to southernmost towns.

n: Ish-bosheth, completely dependent on Abner, is too afraid to say anything back. The scene shows how hollow his kingship is.
Abner opens secret negotiations with David, offering to bring all Israel over to him if David will make a covenant with him.

f.g: A rhetorical question, perhaps meaning “Who really controls the land?” — implying Abner does.
A covenant or treaty.

n: David agrees, but on one condition: Abner must bring back Michal, Saul’s daughter and David’s first wife. Restoring her would strengthen David’s legal tie to Saul’s house.
David also makes a formal request to Ish-bosheth, reminding him that he paid Saul a costly bride-price for Michal.

f.g: Espoused = betrothed, or formally married.

f.w: an hundred foreskins of the Philistines
f.g: Saul had asked for 100; David brought 200.

n: Ish-bosheth complies, taking Michal from the man Saul had given her to after David fled.

f.g: Also spelled Phalti.

n: A heartbreaking detail: her second husband follows her, weeping, until Abner orders him home. The politics of kings cause real human suffering.

f.g: A village near the Mount of Olives, east of Jerusalem, on the road toward Judah.

n: Abner lobbies the leaders of the northern tribes, reminding them that they had long wanted David as their king.

f.g: The senior men who led clans and tribes.

n: He cites a promise from the Lord that David would save Israel from the Philistines and other enemies — something Saul had failed to do.

f.w: By the hand of my servant David

n: Abner speaks especially to Benjamin, Saul’s own tribe, whose support mattered most. Then he travels to Hebron to report the agreements to David.

f.g: An idiom meaning to speak directly and personally to someone.

n: David receives Abner and twenty men with a feast — a traditional way of sealing a covenant of friendship.

f.w: made Abner and the men that were with him a feast

n: Abner promises to rally all Israel to make a covenant with David as king. David sends him away “in peace” — under his protection.

f.g: Repeated three times (verses 21-23), stressing that David had guaranteed Abner’s safety.

n: Just as Abner leaves, Joab returns from a raid with plunder. The timing sets up the tragedy.

f.g: A raiding band.

n: Joab is told that Abner — the man who killed his brother Asahel — has just been in Hebron and left peacefully.
Joab angrily confronts the king, scolding him for letting Abner go.

f.g: He has gotten clean away.

n: Joab claims Abner was really a spy. His true motives are likely revenge for Asahel and fear of losing his own place as commander to Abner.

f.w: thy going out and thy coming in
f.g: A Hebrew idiom for all of a person’s activities and movements.

n: Without David’s knowledge, Joab sends messengers to call Abner back.

f.g: A site a little north of Hebron.

n: Under the pretense of a private conversation at the city gate, Joab stabs Abner to death — in the same place Abner had struck Asahel. Hebron was a city of refuge, which makes the murder even more shocking.

f.g: Hebron was a city of refuge, where a manslayer was supposed to receive a fair hearing.

n: David publicly declares that he and his kingdom are innocent of Abner’s death. It was crucial that Israel not think David had arranged the killing.
David pronounces a curse on Joab’s family line: may it always suffer disease, weakness, violence, or poverty.

f.g: A bodily discharge; a chronic disease that made one ritually unclean (Leviticus 15).
Possibly a cripple, or, as some translate, one who works a spindle — doing “women’s work,” an insult in that culture.

n: The narrator explains the motive plainly: Joab and Abishai killed Abner to avenge Asahel. But Asahel died in battle, which made this personal revenge, not lawful justice.
David orders everyone, including Joab, to mourn publicly. The king himself walks behind the funeral bier, honoring Abner.

f.g: Coarse cloth, often of goat hair, worn as a sign of grief or repentance.
The frame on which a body was carried to burial.

n: Abner is buried in Hebron, and David weeps aloud at the grave. His grief is sincere and visible to all.
David composes a short lament asking whether Abner died like a “fool” — a reckless, senseless man.

f.g: Hebrew nabal — a morally foolish person (the same word as Nabal’s name in 1 Samuel 25).

n: Abner was no criminal in chains; he was a free man struck down by treachery. The people weep again.

f.g: Shackles for the feet.

n: David refuses to eat until sunset, fasting for Abner even when people urge him to eat.

f.g: In KJV English, “meat” means food in general.

n: The people notice and approve. David’s sincere conduct wins the trust of the nation.

f.w: whatsoever the king did pleased all the people

n: Everyone — Judah and the northern tribes alike — understands that the king had no part in Abner’s murder. This was essential for uniting the kingdom.
David honors Abner as a “prince and a great man” — a generous tribute to a former enemy.

f.g: A leader or commander, not necessarily a king’s son.

n: David admits his weakness: his violent nephews are too strong for him to control. He leaves their punishment to God; Solomon will later deal with Joab.

f.w: the sons of Zeruiah be too hard for me
the LORD shall reward the doer of evil
